questions.q_athlete: You've just been handed a detailed new training programme. What's your honest first move?
questions.q_coach: You hand them a detailed new programme. What do they tend to do?

options.athlete: I study every movement and cue — I want to understand the mechanics before I start.
options.coach: Study every movement and cue — they want the mechanics before they start.

options.athlete: I push back until I understand the reasoning behind the exercise choices.
options.coach: Push back until they understand the reasoning behind your choices.

options.athlete: I just want to know how this makes me better on the competition floor — skip the filler.
options.coach: Skim past the detail — they only care how it makes them better on the floor.

options.athlete: I read it once, trust the coach, and get straight to work.
options.coach: Read it once, trust you, and get straight to work.

questions.q_athlete: You make a visible mistake at a crucial moment in training. What actually happens in your head?
questions.q_coach: They make a visible mistake at a crucial moment. How do they respond?

options.athlete: I spiral — I over-analyse what went wrong and struggle to move on.
options.coach: They spiral — over-analysing the error and struggling to move on.

options.athlete: I hate looking bad in front of people, so I quietly avoid that movement for a while.
options.coach: They hate looking bad, so they quietly avoid that movement for a while.

options.athlete: I use it as fuel. I've been underestimated before — I just grind harder.
options.coach: They use it as fuel and grind harder — they're used to proving people wrong.

options.athlete: I take full blame, even if it wasn't all mine, because I feel responsible for everyone.
options.coach: They take full blame, even when it isn't all theirs, out of responsibility for the group.

questions.q_athlete: How do you really handle a niggle, soreness, or minor tweak mid-cycle?
questions.q_coach: How do they handle a niggle, soreness, or minor tweak mid-cycle?

options.athlete: I'm hyper-aware of it — I'll keep asking whether it's normal or something serious.
options.coach: Hyper-aware — they keep asking whether it's normal or something serious.

options.athlete: I ignore it completely. Showing weakness isn't an option.
options.coach: They ignore it completely and push through, no matter the cost.

options.athlete: If I'm honest, I've used the odd ache to get out of work I didn't fancy.
options.coach: They use the odd ache to slip out of work they didn't fancy.

options.athlete: I panic a bit — I don't have the experience yet to know what's serious.
options.coach: They get anxious — they don't have the experience to know what's serious.

questions.q_athlete: A new, no-nonsense coach starts barking orders with zero explanation. What's your instinct?
questions.q_coach: A new, no-nonsense coach gives them orders with no explanation. What happens?

options.athlete: Instant distrust. You earn my buy-in before I give it.
options.coach: Instant distrust — you have to earn their buy-in before they give it.

options.athlete: I rebel internally. I want options, not orders.
options.coach: They rebel internally — they want options, not orders.

options.athlete: I work out what they want to hear so I can stay under the radar.
options.coach: They work out what the coach wants to hear and stay under the radar.

options.athlete: If it matches what a top athlete or coach online does, I'm in. Otherwise I doubt it.
options.coach: They'll follow if it matches what a top athlete or online coach does, otherwise they doubt it.

questions.q_athlete: What's your natural role in the room right before a big session or competition?
questions.q_coach: What's their natural role in the room before a big session or competition?

options.athlete: I'm the loudest — I make sure the energy's up and everyone notices.
options.coach: The loudest — making sure the energy's up and everyone notices them.

options.athlete: I'm quietly checking in on people — I'm the glue that holds us together.
options.coach: Quietly checking in on teammates — the emotional glue.

options.athlete: I sit on my own and get focused. I don't need anyone else to perform.
options.coach: On their own, fiercely self-contained — they don't need anyone to perform.

options.athlete: I keep it light and fun — I play best when I'm enjoying it, not when it's heavy.
options.coach: Keeping it light and fun — they perform best when they're enjoying it.

questions.q_athlete: Which statement is closest to the truth about your physical talent?
questions.q_coach: Which best describes their relationship with their own physical talent?

options.athlete: I don't have natural gifts — I just out-work everyone.
options.coach: Limited natural gifts, but they out-work everyone.

options.athlete: I've got the tools, but I struggle to fully believe in myself when it counts.
options.coach: Real physical tools, but their self-belief comes and goes when it counts.

options.athlete: My genetics have carried me — I've never really needed structured prep.
options.coach: Heavily reliant on genetics — they doubt they need structured prep.

options.athlete: I've got real tools and I hold myself to the highest standard to set the example.
options.coach: Strong tools and they hold themselves to the highest standard for the group.

questions.q_athlete: When training gets repetitive or monotonous, what's most likely to happen?
questions.q_coach: When training gets repetitive or monotonous, what do they do?

options.athlete: I keep going. Routine is a feature, not a bug.
options.coach: Keep going — routine is a feature, not a bug, for them.

options.athlete: I start looking for ways around the plan — a swap here, a shortcut there.
options.coach: Start finding ways around the plan — swaps, shortcuts, their own terms.

options.athlete: I lose motivation fast. Variety and creativity are what keep me locked in.
options.coach: Lose motivation fast — variety and creativity are what keep them engaged.

options.athlete: I start looking at what other coaches or athletes are doing instead.
options.coach: Start eyeing what other coaches or athletes are doing instead.

questions.q_athlete: How would the people who train alongside you describe you?
questions.q_coach: How would their training partners describe them?

options.athlete: Intense and technical — always analysing, sometimes too much.
options.coach: Intense and technical — always analysing, sometimes too much.

options.athlete: The loudest one in the room — not always for the right reasons.
options.coach: The loudest in the room — not always for the right reasons.

options.athlete: Quietly reliable, but does things their own way — don't get in the way.
options.coach: Quietly reliable but does things their own way — don't get in the way.

options.athlete: Infectious energy — makes training fun and pulls people up.
options.coach: Infectious energy — makes training fun and lifts the room.

questions.q_athlete: A coach challenges your approach and tells you to change something. Your honest response?
questions.q_coach: You challenge their approach and tell them to change something. Their honest reaction?

options.athlete: I need to know exactly why they're right before I change anything.
options.coach: They need to know exactly why you're right before they'll change.

options.athlete: I feel defensive and embarrassed, especially if people are watching.
options.coach: They get defensive and embarrassed, especially with people watching.

options.athlete: I'll say I'll change it, then mostly do what I was going to do anyway.
options.coach: They agree to your face, then mostly carry on as before.

options.athlete: I take it hard — I internalise it and replay it for hours.
options.coach: They take it hard — internalising it and replaying it for hours.

questions.q_athlete: What do you most need from a coach to do your best work?
questions.q_coach: What does this athlete most need from you to do their best work?

options.athlete: Context and reasoning — I want the thinking behind the decisions.
options.coach: Context and reasoning — the thinking behind the decisions.

options.athlete: Autonomy and variety — fewer rigid rules.
options.coach: Autonomy and variety — fewer rigid rules.

options.athlete: Patience — I'm still figuring this out.
options.coach: Patience — they're still finding their feet.

options.athlete: Consistency — earn my trust before expecting me to give it.
options.coach: Consistency — they need you to earn trust before they give it.

questions.q_athlete: A hard benchmark's coming up and you're not sure you'll score well. What do you honestly do?
questions.q_coach: A hard benchmark's coming and they might not score well. What do they tend to do?

options.athlete: I find a reason to sit it out or do it off to the side. I'd rather not post a number I'm not proud of.
options.coach: Find a reason to sit it out or do it quietly. They'd rather not post a number they're not proud of.

options.athlete: I want to smash it, but I tighten up and get in my own head when it actually counts.
options.coach: Want to smash it, but tighten up and overthink when it counts.

options.athlete: I know the engine's there. I've just got to back myself to go with the top group.
options.coach: Have the tools, it's the self-belief that comes and goes on the day.

options.athlete: I set the standard anyway and expect everyone else to bring it too.
options.coach: Set the standard anyway and hold the room to it.

questions.q_athlete: This block pulls you away from your main event into general prep. How do you take it?
questions.q_coach: The block pulls them off their main event into general prep. How do they take it?

options.athlete: If it doesn't obviously make me better at my sport, it feels like a distraction.
options.coach: If it doesn't obviously serve their sport, it feels like a distraction.

options.athlete: I'll get bored fast unless there's variety and something to enjoy in it.
options.coach: They lose interest fast without variety and enjoyment.

options.athlete: I want to understand exactly how this accessory work transfers before I buy in.
options.coach: They want to understand exactly how it transfers before committing.

options.athlete: I'll grind through anything as long as it's honest work.
options.coach: They'll grind through anything as long as it's honest graft.

questions.q_athlete: Someone in the group is clearly having a rough session. What are you most likely doing?
questions.q_coach: Someone's having a rough session. What are they most likely doing?

options.athlete: Checking in on them. I can feel the room and I want everyone alright.
options.coach: Checking in on them, reading the room, wanting everyone okay.

options.athlete: Loud and rallying everyone, bringing the energy up.
options.coach: Loud, rallying the room, bringing energy.

options.athlete: Head down on my own work. I look after me.
options.coach: Head down on their own work, looking after themselves.

options.athlete: Quietly getting on with my own session, my own way.
options.coach: Quietly doing their own session their own way.

questions.q_athlete: You've been carrying a small injury for a couple of weeks. What's the honest truth?
questions.q_coach: They've been carrying a small injury for weeks. What's the honest picture?

options.athlete: I keep googling it and asking whether it's something serious.
options.coach: They keep checking it and asking whether it's serious.

options.athlete: I train straight through it and don't make a thing of it.
options.coach: They train through it and don't mention it.

options.athlete: If I'm honest, I might lean on it to duck work I don't fancy.
options.coach: They may lean on it to avoid work they don't fancy.

options.athlete: I'm not sure what's normal yet, so it makes me anxious.
options.coach: They're unsure what's normal, so it makes them anxious.

questions.q_athlete: Your coach praises you in front of the whole group. How does it sit with you?
questions.q_coach: The coach praises them in front of the group. How does it sit?

options.athlete: I love it. How I'm seen matters to me.
options.coach: They enjoy it, reputation and standing matter to them.

options.athlete: I feed off it. More attention, more energy.
options.coach: They feed off it, attention lifts their energy.

options.athlete: I deflect it to the group. We did that together.
options.coach: They deflect credit to the group.

options.athlete: It makes me self-conscious and I start overthinking my next rep.
options.coach: It makes them self-conscious and they overthink what's next.

questions.q_athlete: It's the big day and everything's on the line. What's going on inside?
questions.q_coach: Big day, everything on the line. What's going on for them?

options.athlete: The tools are all there. Whether I believe it today is the variable.
options.coach: The tools are there, self-belief is the variable that day.

options.athlete: I overthink it and can freeze right when it matters most.
options.coach: They overthink and can freeze when it matters.

options.athlete: I'm scanning my body for every twinge, half-expecting something to go wrong.
options.coach: They scan their body for twinges, half-expecting something to go wrong.

options.athlete: This is my whole identity. There's more riding on it for me than most.
options.coach: Their identity is bound up in it, more rides on it for them.

questions.q_athlete: A rest day lands in your programme. What actually happens?
questions.q_coach: A rest day lands. What actually happens?

options.athlete: Rest feels like weakness. I struggle to sit still and do nothing.
options.coach: Rest feels like weakness, they struggle to sit still.

options.athlete: I obsess over whether I've recovered enough to go again.
options.coach: They obsess over whether they've recovered enough.

options.athlete: I'll only rest if it clearly helps my competition performance.
options.coach: They'll only rest if it clearly serves competition.

options.athlete: Rest's fine. I'll go and do something fun instead.
options.coach: Rest's fine, they'll go do something fun.

questions.q_athlete: You get paired with a talented training partner who coasts. What do you do?
questions.q_coach: They're paired with a talented partner who coasts. What do they do?

options.athlete: It winds me up. I out-work them to make a point.
options.coach: It winds them up, they out-work the partner to prove it.

options.athlete: I try to pull their standard up to mine.
options.coach: They try to lift the partner's standard to theirs.

options.athlete: I try to bring them in and get them connected to the group.
options.coach: They try to connect the partner into the group.

options.athlete: I work out how to get what I need out of the pairing.
options.coach: They work out how to get what they need from it.

questions.q_athlete: A coach gives you detailed technical feedback. How do you take it in?
questions.q_coach: The coach gives detailed technical feedback. How do they take it?

options.athlete: I love it. Give me every cue and the mechanics behind it.
options.coach: They love it, they want every cue and the mechanics.

options.athlete: It can overwhelm me. I need it kept simple.
options.coach: It can overwhelm them, they need it simple.

options.athlete: Keep it short and execution-focused, don't overload me.
options.coach: Keep it short and execution-focused, don't overload them.

options.athlete: If it's picked apart in front of others, it stings.
options.coach: Feedback in front of others stings them.

questions.q_athlete: You disagree with something in the plan. What do you genuinely do?
questions.q_coach: They disagree with something in the plan. What do they genuinely do?

options.athlete: I quietly do my own thing and route around it.
options.coach: They quietly route around it and do their own thing.

options.athlete: I challenge it head-on and ask for the reasoning.
options.coach: They challenge it directly and ask for the reasoning.

options.athlete: I do it my own way. I don't need telling twice.
options.coach: They do it their own way, self-sufficient about it.

options.athlete: I say the right things, then do what I was going to do.
options.coach: They say the right things, then do their own thing.

questions.q_athlete: What actually keeps you training over the long haul?
questions.q_coach: What actually keeps them training long term?

options.athlete: Enjoyment. The day it stops being fun, I start to drift.
options.coach: Enjoyment, they drift when it stops being fun.

options.athlete: Chasing the sport itself. Competing is the whole point.
options.coach: Chasing the sport, competing is the point.

options.athlete: The people, and being part of something bigger than the result.
options.coach: The people and being part of something bigger.

options.athlete: The grind. Proving I can out-work anyone in the room.
options.coach: The grind, proving they out-work the room.

questions.q_athlete: First few weeks in a new gym or programme. What are you like?
questions.q_coach: First weeks in a new gym. What are they like?

options.athlete: Keen but a bit overwhelmed, everything's new.
options.coach: Keen but overwhelmed, everything's new.

options.athlete: I keep to myself until people earn my trust.
options.coach: They keep to themselves until trust is earned.

options.athlete: I'm vocal and make myself known quickly.
options.coach: They're vocal and make themselves known fast.

options.athlete: Every new stimulus has me wondering how my body will hold up.
options.coach: New stimulus has them worrying how their body holds up.
